screens.title: Typical Container CI/CD Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A container CI/CD pipeline on AWS is a sequence of stages that convert a commit into a running service. The first stage is source: a commit to CodeCommit, GitHub, or Bitbucket triggers the pipeline. Next, CodeBuild runs the build stage: it checks out code, builds the Docker image according to your Dockerfile, runs unit tests, and tags the image. After a successful build, CodeBuild pushes the image to ECR and writes an imagedefinitions. json artifact that names the container and the pushed image URI. The test stage deploys that image to a transient environment like a staging ECS service or an EKS namespace where integration and end-to-end tests and vulnerability scans run. Finally, the deployment stage promotes the validated image to production using CodeDeploy or a direct update to ECS/EKS. Common misconceptions include thinking builds only produce binaries; with containers they also produce immutable image artifacts that must be tagged and stored. A practical check: ensure your pipeline emits imagedefinitions. json and confirm the image appears in ECR before proceeding. This pipeline pattern gives repeatability and a single trusted image for all subsequent stages.

content.html:
Core Concept

Typical CI/CD Workflow

A repeatable chain from commit to production with a single image artifact.

1. Source: Commit triggers pipeline
2. Build: CodeBuild builds, tests, tags image
3. Test: Deploy to staging for integration and scans
4. Deploy: CodeDeploy/ECS/EKS to production
Key Takeaway

Design the pipeline so the image pushed to ECR is the exact artifact tested and deployed.

Process Flow
Source
CodeCommit/GitHub trigger
Build
CodeBuild: Docker build & tag
Test
Staging deploy & scans
Deploy
CodeDeploy/ECS/EKS
Artifact and verification
  • CodeBuild pushes an image to ECR and writes imagedefinitions.json for deployments.
  • Staging runs integration tests and vulnerability scans to validate the image.
  • Only a validated image is promoted to production to ensure consistency.
Example
A commit triggers CodePipeline; CodeBuild outputs an image tagged with the commit hash; the image appears in ECR and the pipeline pauses if the scan finds high-severity vulnerabilities.

screens.title: Source Stage and Pipeline Triggers
screens.narratorSegment: The source stage is where the automation begins. A commit to a repository such as CodeCommit, GitHub, or Bitbucket triggers CodePipeline to start downstream stages. This trigger can be immediate via webhooks or polled periodically depending on your provider configuration. The source stage's job is to capture the exact code revision that will be built so that the resulting image is traceable to a commit hash. A common pitfall is assuming a branch name alone is sufficient; by using the commit hash as the image tag you maintain immutability and clear traceability between source and the deployed container. Another practical detail is authentication: CodePipeline must have permissions to pull from your source or you must configure a connection. For GitHub you typically create a connection in the console; for CodeCommit the pipeline already integrates within the account. Finally, consider ephemeral branches for feature testing: the same pipeline pattern supports pull-request builds and temporary environments, but ensure you clean up temporary staging resources. Ask yourself: can I map every running container back to a commit and build artifact? Source Stage and Pipeline Triggers means use commit hashes and source-triggered pipelines so deployed images map directly to specific code revisions.. In practical terms, how commits start the automated workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition

Source Stage & Triggers

Commits or PR events start the pipeline and pin the revision used to build images.

Why it matters: ensures traceability from running container back to source commit.
Common mistake: tagging images only with branch names loses immutability and traceability.
Practical check: tag images with the short commit hash and verify it in ECR.
Examples & Scenarios
GitHub PR Build
A PR triggers a build that deploys to a temporary staging environment for review.
CodeCommit Main Branch
Commits to main trigger full pipeline including production deployment gates.
Pro Tip

Configure your pipeline to pass the commit hash into the build environment so tagging is deterministic.

screens.title: CodeBuild: Building, Tagging, and Pushing Images
screens.narratorSegment: CodeBuild is the service that compiles, tests, and creates container images in this pipeline. You configure a project with an environment image that includes Docker and enable privileged mode so Docker can run inside the build container. The build is driven by a buildspec. yaml that defines pre_build, build, and post_build phases. In pre_build you authenticate to ECR and compute a tag, often using the short commit hash. During build you run docker build and create tags such as the commit hash and latest. In post_build you push images to ECR and write imagedefinitions. json so downstream steps know which image to deploy. It's important that the CodeBuild role has the exact ECR permissions required and that artifacts are uploaded to S3 for CodePipeline to pick up. A common misunderstanding is thinking CodeBuild automatically publishes images; you must explicitly docker push and produce the artifact. As a practical exercise, create a CodeBuild project with privileged mode enabled, run the build, and verify the pushed tags and imagedefinitions. json in the artifacts ZIP. CodeBuild: Build, Tag, Push

Configure an image with Docker, enable privileged mode, and provide a buildspec to produce and push images.

screens.title: buildspec.yaml — Example and Explanation
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine a concrete buildspec. yaml and explain each phase so you can adapt it to your projects. The provided buildspec defines pre_build commands where the build agent prints the AWS CLI version and authenticates to ECR using the get-login-password flow. It then sets REPOSITORY_URI and computes IMAGE_TAG from the resolved source version, typically the commit hash. In the build phase it runs docker build to create the image and docker tag to prepare both a commit-hash tag and a latest tag. The post_build phase pushes both tags to ECR and prints a JSON file with the container name and pushed image URI into imagedefinitions. json, which CodePipeline will use. Artifacts then include imagedefinitions. json so CodeDeploy can update ECS task definitions. A common error is forgetting to enable privileged mode for Docker builds; without it the docker build will fail in the CodeBuild environment. Also ensure the role can call ecr:GetAuthorizationToken and put images. keyIdea.title: Buildspec purpose
keyIdea.text: A buildspec defines exact commands for building, tagging, pushing images, and creating deployment artifacts like imagedefinitions.json.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

buildspec.yaml Example

This buildspec logs into ECR, builds and tags the Docker image, pushes it, and writes imagedefinitions.json.

version: 0.2

phases:
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - echo Logging in to Amazon ECR...
      - aws --version
      - $(aws ecr get-login-password --region $AWS_DEFAULT_REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $AWS_ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION.amazonaws.com)
      - REPOSITORY_URI=$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION.amazonaws.com/$IMAGE_REPO_NAME
      - IMAGE_TAG=$(echo $CODEBUILD_RESOLVED_SOURCE_VERSION | cut -c 1-7)

  build:
    commands:
      - echo Build started on `date`
      - echo Building the Docker image...
      - docker build -t $IMAGE_REPO_NAME:$IMAGE_TAG .
      - docker tag $IMAGE_REPO_NAME:$IMAGE_TAG $REPOSITORY_URI:$IMAGE_TAG
      - docker tag $IMAGE_REPO_NAME:$IMAGE_TAG $REPOSITORY_URI:latest

  post_build:
    commands:
      - echo Build completed on `date`
      - echo Pushing the Docker images...
      - docker push $REPOSITORY_URI:$IMAGE_TAG
      - docker push $REPOSITORY_URI:latest
      - echo Writing image definitions file...
      - printf '[{"name":"%s","imageUri":"%s"}]' $CONTAINER_NAME $REPOSITORY_URI:$IMAGE_TAG > imagedefinitions.json
artifacts:
    files:
      - imagedefinitions.json
Pre-build
Auth to ECR and compute tag.
Build
docker build and tag both commit and latest.
Post-build
Push images and write imagedefinitions.json artifact.

screens.title: ECR, Tagging, and imagedefinitions.json
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Elastic Container Registry is the OCI-compliant image store where your build pushes images. When CodeBuild tags an image with the short commit hash and latest, the commit tag gives you traceability while latest gives a convenience pointer. For deployments to ECS using CodeDeploy and CodePipeline, imagedefinitions. json is the simple JSON artifact that maps a container name in the task definition to the exact image URI you just pushed. This file typically looks like a one-item array with name and imageUri fields. CodePipeline picks this artifact up and CodeDeploy uses it to create a new task definition revision or update an existing one. A common misunderstanding is thinking CodeDeploy reads tags directly from ECR; instead, CodeDeploy relies on the imagedefinitions. json artifact passed through the pipeline. Practically, verify that your build artifacts ZIP contains imagedefinitions. json and that the image URI in the file matches the image visible in the ECR console. This pattern ensures the deployed task definition references a known, tested image. ECR, Tagging, and imagedefinitions.json means imagedefinitions.json is the linkage between the built image and the ecs task definition used for deployment.. In practical terms, how images are stored, referenced, and passed to deployments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

ECR, Tagging & imagedefinitions.json

Store immutable images in ECR and pass the exact image URI to the deployment step via a simple JSON artifact.

Tagging: Commit-hash tags for immutability; latest for convenience but avoid relying on it for rollback.
Artifact: imagedefinitions.json maps container name to the image URI for CodeDeploy.
Check: Ensure the artifact in S3 contains the expected imageUri before deployment.
Example imagedefinitions.json
[{"name":"my-web-app-container","imageUri":"123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-web-app:abc1234"}]
Why imagedefinitions.json?
It creates a stable contract between the build and deployment stages so the exact image is deployed, not an inferred tag.

screens.title: Testing Stage and Staging Deployments
screens.narratorSegment: After a build produces an image and imagedefinitions. json, a test stage exercises that image in an environment that mirrors production. This may be a staging ECS service or an EKS namespace that receives the new image. Integration tests, end-to-end tests, and security scans run here to validate behavior under real runtime conditions. The goal is to find regressions and vulnerabilities before they reach users. A common pitfall is relying only on unit tests during the build; container behavior often depends on runtime configuration, networking, and external services, so integration tests in staging catch issues unit tests miss. Also, ensure your staging environment uses the same task definitions, resource limits, and load balancer configuration as production when possible. If the staging tests or scans fail, the pipeline should block progression to deployment. This gating increases confidence and makes advanced deployment strategies meaningful because the image arriving in production is already validated. Testing Stage and Staging Deployments means use a staging deployment to validate runtime behavior and scans before promoting an image to production.. In practical terms, deploying images to test environments and gating production. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow

Testing & Staging Deployments

screens.title: Vulnerability Scanning for Container Images
screens.narratorSegment: Vulnerability scanning finds known security flaws in container images before they reach production. Amazon ECR provides built-in image scanning powered by Amazon Inspector which you can enable per repository to automatically scan images on push. The scan returns findings by severity, and you can configure your pipeline to pause or fail if audits exceed an acceptable threshold. For more control or earlier detection, run a scanner like Trivy or Clair inside CodeBuild during the test stage; this gives you custom rules and richer reporting. A typical integration runs a scan after the image is built but before it's promoted; if critical vulnerabilities are detected, the pipeline rejects the image. A misconception is that scanning alone is sufficient: it must be paired with patching or base-image updates and a policy defining which severities block deployments. Finally, ensure you store scan results in a place your team can review, and automate alerts when new critical issues are discovered so you can remediate proactively. screens.title: Orchestrating with CodePipeline and CodeDeploy
screens.narratorSegment: CodePipeline is the conductor that links source, build, test, and deploy stages together. It invokes CodeBuild for building and testing and passes artifacts such as imagedefinitions. json to CodeDeploy to perform the actual rollout. CodeDeploy supports Blue/Green and Canary deployment mechanisms for ECS and integrates with ALB for traffic shifting. When setting up this orchestration, ensure your pipeline artifact structure includes both the image artifact and any appspec or deployment configuration CodeDeploy needs. screens.title: Blue/Green Deployments for ECS and EKS
screens.narratorSegment: Blue/Green deployment runs two parallel production environments: Blue is the current live version and Green is the new version you want to release. For ECS, CodeDeploy creates a new set of tasks for Green, uses an Application Load Balancer to shift traffic from Blue to Green, and then terminates Blue when the process succeeds. For EKS, CodeDeploy can work with the AWS Load Balancer Controller to move traffic between two Kubernetes services that represent Blue and Green. The major advantage is an instantaneous rollback path: if monitoring detects errors, traffic can be returned to Blue quickly. Common misconceptions include thinking Blue/Green always doubles cost; you can limit Green's capacity until validated or use scaled-down Green environments for smoke testing. Also plan for stateful data migrations carefully because switching services does not migrate data by itself. Use CloudWatch alarms tied to error rates and latency during the traffic shift so CodeDeploy can automatically revert on failure. Blue/Green is an excellent pattern when you need predictable cutovers and immediate recovery. Blue/Green Deployments for ECS and EKS means blue/green deployment provides a fast recovery path by switching traffic between two identical environments managed by codedeploy.. In practical terms, two identical environments with traffic switching for zero-downtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Blue/Green deployment provides a fast recovery path by switching traffic between two identical environments managed by CodeDeploy.

content.html:
Comparison

Blue/Green: ECS vs EKS

Both run parallel environments; traffic is shifted to the new version once validated.

ECS: CodeDeploy creates a Green task set and shifts traffic via ALB, then removes Blue tasks.
EKS: Use CodeDeploy with the Load Balancer Controller or external tools to shift between services.
Watchouts: prepare for data migrations and reduce Green capacity if cost is a concern.
Deployment Steps
  1. Deploy Green environment and run smoke tests.
  2. Shift a percentage of traffic to Green and monitor alarms.
  3. On success, shift all traffic and terminate Blue; on failure, revert instantly to Blue.
Example: CodeDeploy for ECS will create a new task set and use ALB routing to move traffic, then automatically rollback if CloudWatch alerts exceed thresholds during the shift.

screens.title: Canary Deployments and Automated Rollback
screens.narratorSegment: Canary deployments roll out a new version to a small subset of users first, so you get real-user feedback while limiting blast radius. For ECS, CodeDeploy supports linear or canary traffic shifting where a small percentage of traffic goes to the new task set initially. For EKS, service meshes or tools like Flagger or Istio perform advanced canary routing. The essential ingredients are monitoring, gradual shifts, and a rollback plan. Configure CloudWatch alarms on key metrics such as 5xx errors or latency. If thresholds are breached, CodeDeploy can automatically roll back traffic to the previous known-good version. A common misconception is that canaries replace testing; they complement testing by providing real-user validation. Also decide what percentage and duration for canaries based on traffic patterns and business risk. Finally, automate rollback actions and run drills so the team knows how to respond when alarms fire. Canary plus automated rollback is a pragmatic way to validate behavior in production while keeping users protected. Canary Deployments and Automated Rollback means canary releases expose a small portion of traffic to the new version and use alarms to trigger rollback if problems surface.. In practical terms, gradual rollout with monitoring and immediate revert on failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.text: Canary releases expose a small portion of traffic to the new version and use alarms to trigger rollback if problems surface.

content.html:
Comparison

Canary Deployments & Rollback

Roll out changes gradually and monitor production metrics to decide whether to advance or revert.

Canary: shift a small percentage, observe behavior, then increase traffic if healthy.
Rollback: use CloudWatch alarms to trigger automated reversion via CodeDeploy or Lambda.
Misconception: canaries do not replace testing; they provide real traffic validation.
Checklist for Canary
  • Define initial traffic percentage and observation window.
  • Set CloudWatch alarms for error rates and latency that should trigger rollback.
  • Automate rollback and document manual rollback steps as a fallback.
Example: shift 5% of traffic for 15 minutes; if 5xx rate exceeds the threshold, CodeDeploy reverts traffic immediately to the previous version.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the three essential concepts to carry forward. First, treat the pushed ECR image as the canonical artifact: build once, test once, and deploy the exact image everywhere. Second, use the pipeline to gate promotion with automated tests and image scanning; failing on high-severity findings prevents risky images from reaching production. Third, choose a safe deployment strategy — Blue/Green for near-instant rollback or Canary for gradual exposure — and wire CloudWatch alarms and automated rollback so production can recover quickly. These principles together let teams ship changes frequently while maintaining control and security. When you design your pipeline, map how each stage reads and writes artifacts, and define clear policies for scanning severity thresholds and rollback triggers. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll walk through a complete container CI/CD workflow on AWS and why each step matters. You will learn how source commits trigger builds, how CodeBuild creates and tags Docker images, and how those images are pushed to Amazon ECR for downstream deployment. We'll also cover how to include vulnerability scanning so images are verified before deployment, and how advanced strategies like Blue/Green and Canary releases reduce downtime and risk. A practical artifact, imagedefinitions. json, connects builds to deployments, and CodeDeploy orchestrates safe traffic shifts and automated rollbacks when alarms detect problems. Throughout, we'll emphasize the permissions and testing you need so automation stays secure and reliable. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to design a pipeline that builds, scans, stores, and safely deploys container images to ECS or EKS, and you will know where to add tests and alarms to protect production. Think about a small feature change: this pipeline should let you ship it with confidence while providing fast rollback if something goes wrong.

These objectives define the practical skills you'll build in this chapter. First, you'll design and implement a CI/CD pipeline for containerized applications using AWS Developer Tools, focusing on a complete workflow from commit to production. Second, you'll automate building, tagging, and pushing Docker images to Amazon ECR using CodeBuild and an appropriate buildspec file, creating artifacts that downstream steps can consume. Third, you'll integrate vulnerability scanning into the pipeline so images are validated before they reach staging or production, and you'll learn how to fail a pipeline on critical findings. Fourth, you'll implement advanced deployment strategies such as Blue/Green and Canary and understand how CodeDeploy coordinates traffic shifts and tests. Each objective includes hands-on actions and checks so you can demonstrate competency in a real AWS account environment. As you progress, reflect on why automation and testing increase confidence and how least-privilege IAM helps keep your pipeline secure.

These additional objectives focus on the practical artifacts and safety practices you must include in real pipelines. You will create the imagedefinitions. json artifact so CodeDeploy can update ECS task definitions automatically. You will enable and interpret ECR image scanning results or run a scanning tool in your build stage to block dangerous images. You will configure CloudWatch alarms tied to deployment health metrics and wire them into automatic rollback behavior via CodeDeploy or Lambda triggers. Finally, you'll apply least-privilege IAM roles so build and deployment services only have the permissions they need. Together, these skills let you move quickly without accepting unnecessary risk: builds are reproducible, images are checked, rollbacks can be automatic, and permissions are constrained. Practice these steps in a lab to validate logs, ECR image visibility, and artifact presence in S3.

A container CI/CD pipeline on AWS is a sequence of stages that convert a commit into a running service. The first stage is source: a commit to CodeCommit, GitHub, or Bitbucket triggers the pipeline. Next, CodeBuild runs the build stage: it checks out code, builds the Docker image according to your Dockerfile, runs unit tests, and tags the image. After a successful build, CodeBuild pushes the image to ECR and writes an imagedefinitions. json artifact that names the container and the pushed image URI. The test stage deploys that image to a transient environment like a staging ECS service or an EKS namespace where integration and end-to-end tests and vulnerability scans run. Finally, the deployment stage promotes the validated image to production using CodeDeploy or a direct update to ECS/EKS. Common misconceptions include thinking builds only produce binaries; with containers they also produce immutable image artifacts that must be tagged and stored. A practical check: ensure your pipeline emits imagedefinitions. json and confirm the image appears in ECR before proceeding. This pipeline pattern gives repeatability and a single trusted image for all subsequent stages.

The source stage is where the automation begins. A commit to a repository such as CodeCommit, GitHub, or Bitbucket triggers CodePipeline to start downstream stages. This trigger can be immediate via webhooks or polled periodically depending on your provider configuration. The source stage's job is to capture the exact code revision that will be built so that the resulting image is traceable to a commit hash. A common pitfall is assuming a branch name alone is sufficient; by using the commit hash as the image tag you maintain immutability and clear traceability between source and the deployed container. Another practical detail is authentication: CodePipeline must have permissions to pull from your source or you must configure a connection. For GitHub you typically create a connection in the console; for CodeCommit the pipeline already integrates within the account. Finally, consider ephemeral branches for feature testing: the same pipeline pattern supports pull-request builds and temporary environments, but ensure you clean up temporary staging resources. Ask yourself: can I map every running container back to a commit and build artifact? Source Stage and Pipeline Triggers means use commit hashes and source-triggered pipelines so deployed images map directly to specific code revisions.. In practical terms, how commits start the automated workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CodeBuild is the service that compiles, tests, and creates container images in this pipeline. You configure a project with an environment image that includes Docker and enable privileged mode so Docker can run inside the build container. The build is driven by a buildspec. yaml that defines pre_build, build, and post_build phases. In pre_build you authenticate to ECR and compute a tag, often using the short commit hash. During build you run docker build and create tags such as the commit hash and latest. In post_build you push images to ECR and write imagedefinitions. json so downstream steps know which image to deploy. It's important that the CodeBuild role has the exact ECR permissions required and that artifacts are uploaded to S3 for CodePipeline to pick up. A common misunderstanding is thinking CodeBuild automatically publishes images; you must explicitly docker push and produce the artifact. As a practical exercise, create a CodeBuild project with privileged mode enabled, run the build, and verify the pushed tags and imagedefinitions. json in the artifacts ZIP. CodeBuild: Building, Tagging, and Pushing Images means codebuild must both push images to ecr and emit imagedefinitions.json for codedeploy to perform ecs deployments.. In practical terms, how codebuild runs docker builds and produces deployment artifacts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's examine a concrete buildspec. yaml and explain each phase so you can adapt it to your projects. The provided buildspec defines pre_build commands where the build agent prints the AWS CLI version and authenticates to ECR using the get-login-password flow. It then sets REPOSITORY_URI and computes IMAGE_TAG from the resolved source version, typically the commit hash. In the build phase it runs docker build to create the image and docker tag to prepare both a commit-hash tag and a latest tag. The post_build phase pushes both tags to ECR and prints a JSON file with the container name and pushed image URI into imagedefinitions. json, which CodePipeline will use. Artifacts then include imagedefinitions. json so CodeDeploy can update ECS task definitions. A common error is forgetting to enable privileged mode for Docker builds; without it the docker build will fail in the CodeBuild environment. Also ensure the role can call ecr:GetAuthorizationToken and put images. Amazon Elastic Container Registry is the OCI-compliant image store where your build pushes images. When CodeBuild tags an image with the short commit hash and latest, the commit tag gives you traceability while latest gives a convenience pointer. Blue/Green deployment runs two parallel production environments: Blue is the current live version and Green is the new version you want to release. For ECS, CodeDeploy creates a new set of tasks for Green, uses an Application Load Balancer to shift traffic from Blue to Green, and then terminates Blue when the process succeeds. The major advantage is an instantaneous rollback path: if monitoring detects errors, traffic can be returned to Blue quickly.
